entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Imam Ali Mosque, also known as the Imam Ali Shrine, is a paramount Shi'ite mosque and mausoleum located in Najaf, Iraq, which holds profound significance in Islamic history as it is believed to house the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. Established in the 7th century CE, this site not only serves as a center of pilgrimage for millions of Shia Muslims but also embodies the theological and political struggles that shaped early Islamic history and sectarian identities. The mosque's architecture, featuring intricate tile work and grand domes, reflects the artistic achievements of the Islamic Golden Age and signifies the socio-religious importance of Najaf as a center of learning and religious authority.

The mosque's historical foundation was laid shortly after the death of Ali in 661 CE, marking it as a critical site for the Shi'ite community, which emerged in opposition to the Umayyad Caliphate. Over the centuries, the shrine has been expanded and renovated, particularly during the Safavid period in the 16th century, when it became a focal point for Shia religious and political life. The Imam Ali Mosque not only symbolizes the enduring legacy of Ali's teachings but has also been a site of political resistance, notably during the 1920 Iraqi Revolution against British colonial rule, where it served as a rallying point for nationalists and Shia leaders.
